Even some independents in Michigan are nervous about his uberprogressive platform. He will need to win over more than just the far-left to score a victory in November (he barely won his primary), so Monday night he went on Fox News and sat for a lengthy interview with Jesse Watters.

   1. It started out cordial. El-Sayed seemed to know it might get feisty but he offered an olive branch to begin, saying he and Watters had some things in common. “We both played football and lacrosse. We both love America. We both love freedom. And I’m looking forward to that conversation.”

   2. Then they sparred. Watters asked El-Sayed about his proposal to abolish the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. El-Sayed started talking about the country’s 250th anniversary and getting rid of tyranny and how ICE had killed people. He sounded a bit like a politician, and Watters cut him off. “Yeah, but that’s a dodge, Abdul.” El-Sayed didn’t lose his cool but kept trying to redirect. “You cut me off, Jesse, you said we’re going to have a good conversation. I’d like to do that.”

   3. It got personal: They were talking about transgender surgery, and it became intense. Watters kept pressing, saying, “So you think it’s OK for a parent to slash his kid’s ding-a-ling off?” El-Sayed responded: “Are you circumcised?” Watters said, “Yeah, but that’s a personal question, Doctor!” El-Sayed was trying to make the point that a lot of personal medical decisions are made between families and doctors. Watters said that “circumcision is different than castration.”

   4. Shariah law: Watters pressed El-Sayed, a Muslim, on whether he supported pushing Shariah law on Americans. “Nobody is trying to push Shariah law on anybody else,” El-Sayed said. “I would never want somebody to push their faith on me, and I would never want to push my faith on someone else.”

Four Takeaways From Abdul El-Sayed’s Wild Fox News Interview
 
Plus, Scott Bessent launches new effort to isolate Iran, and fresh plans for six-figure levy on H1-B visas
 
 
EMILY ELCONIN/BLOOMBERG NEWS
 

Good morning. Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan Democrat running for U.S. Senate, has been a frequent target of criticism by Republicans. What I’m Following

 
 
EVELYN HOCKSTEIN/REUTERS
 

Countries that do business with Iran will feel U.S.’s wrath, warns Scott Bessent. The Treasury secretary launched a new campaign to isolate the Iranian regime, called “Operation Economic Outcast.” Bessent said his department has “mapped every node, every facilitator and every network that Iran has used to smuggle oil and evade sanctions.”

 

Foreign workers face a six-figure fee for new H1-B visas. The Trump administration’s proposal is replacing an earlier plan to charge $100,000 for the visa that was struck down by the courts. The new fees would be levied on all applicants, not just those applying from abroad. If finalized, the move would place a significant new burden on the technology and finance sectors.

 

The battle for the House is being played out in Virginia Beach. Two Navy veterans are battling for Virginia’s Second Congressional District, a bellwether that was won by Trump in 2024 and could decide who controls the House after November’s midterms. The district is one of the roughly 20 most closely fought battlegrounds on the 2026 map and has flipped back and forth between Democrats and Republicans in recent years.

• The Trump administration is planning a mass visa revocation targeting up to 200,000 foreigners who applied for asylum status.

 

• MAGA Inc. threw more than $800,000 on get-out-the-vote calls and text messages in support of Graham.

 

• Trump was warned the war with Iran could be messy, and nearly six months later, a conflict he promised would be over within six weeks has no clear end in sight.
